blocks.text: Most people building with AI in late 2026 understand that the quality of your context determines the quality of your output. But what exactly determines the quality of your context?

inlines.text: Most people building with AI in late 2026 understand that the quality of your context determines the quality of your output. But what exactly determines the quality of your context?

blocks.text: First, let's break down all the different types of context:

inlines.text: First, let's break down all the different types of context:
One-off prompts that you type into chat conversations
Your base instruction files like
AGENTS.md
, injected automatically into each new session
Skill files, which are ideally custom procedural instructions, loaded dynamically as-needed in relevant situations
Word documents and spreadsheets in your Google Drive or similar system
Local markdown files in your code repo
Memories (usually automatically managed by your agent harness and generally not exposed to you visually)

blocks.text: With all these different sources, likely maintained by different people, there's a very high chance you have legacy process docs and out-of-date facts, metrics, decisions, and strategies.

inlines.text: With all these different sources, likely maintained by different people, there's a very high chance you have legacy process docs and out-of-date facts, metrics, decisions, and strategies.

blocks.text: So what happens if your agent finds the wrong information? Or if it finds conflicting information? Doc A says the refund policy is 14 days, Doc B says 30 days. Which one does your agent trust?

inlines.text: So what happens if your agent finds the wrong information? Or if it finds conflicting information? Doc A says the refund policy is 14 days, Doc B says 30 days. Which one does your agent trust?

blocks.text: Context rot vs. context drift

inlines.text: Context rot vs. context drift

blocks.text: People often lump every context issue under context rot, a term coined last year to describe how an LLM's accuracy drops as a session grows too long and fills up with noise, dead ends, and distractors.

inlines.text: People often lump every context issue under
context rot
, a term coined last year to describe how an LLM's accuracy drops as a session grows too long and fills up with noise, dead ends, and distractors.

blocks.text: What happens across a real team's files is slightly different. Over weeks and months, your underlying sources (AGENTS.md, skills, docs, memories, and code) gradually fall out of sync, so your agent can get conflicting instructions on the very first turn of a brand-new session. That's really context drift.

inlines.text: Moving this into my daily coding setup surfaced two quick catches worth knowing:
Logging replaces chat warnings:
Once the tool exists, the agent stops mentioning conflicts in chat (0%) unless you add one line asking for both.
Keep the tool and file list visible up front:

Larger models like Gemini Pro take far fewer exploratory steps than Flash, so they only catch drift in skill or memory files when summaries are listed in the prompt (and when the MCP tool is loaded eagerly rather than hidden behind tool search).

blocks.text: How you act on a logged conflict is up to you. You could pause the agent on the spot, though for everyday work I prefer keeping it passive: the agent logs the file paths, exact quotes, and which version it followed while finishing my task, and I review the cleanup queue later.

blocks.text: Plugging one tiny MCP tool into a local log file gives your agent a built-in sensor for context drift at zero extra cost. Within 24 hours of turning it on in my own setup, it had already caught a real spec-vs-code mismatch during a PR review without me asking.
